This call will be very short, I only have one or two questions." That is what makes them believe you read it.

2. What they have actually been doing, against what the programme says. Pages of plan and not one line about running on the road three times a week on their own decision.

3. What they need from one session. The answer is not treatment. It is to be told whether the repair has failed — and if you do not know that before they arrive, the session will be about something else entirely.
q5key: They believe the repair has failed and nobody has told them otherwise. A good choice is the simple picture you would point at to show where the new pain is coming from and how that differs from the part that was repaired — the picture that answers the question they never wrote down.

title: Walked in yesterday
brief:
New patient. He came to the front desk yesterday and booked in person.
The chart says: "Walk-in. Knee. Booked for tomorrow."
Reception took his details on paper at the desk. Nothing else has reached the system.
First appointment tomorrow at 11:00.

q1.prompt: What do you do before he arrives tomorrow?
opts: Ask reception for the paper sheet they filled in at the desk, read it, and then call him.
Call him and take the whole history from the beginning — the chart is one line, so start from nothing.
Send him the online form so the details are in the system before tomorrow.
Walk-ins are always thin. Take the history in the room tomorrow.
q1.why: About one chart in eleven is a walk-in with nothing written, but the information usually does exist — it is on a sheet at the front desk and nobody typed it in. Two minutes of asking gets you three answers free. Starting the call from nothing means asking him things he already answered standing at the desk, which makes the clinic look disorganised and wastes the part of the call that should go further. Sending the form is worth trying once, but you do not yet know that he has already failed to use it twice. And waiting for the room is a choice to arrive knowing one word.

reveal:
The desk sheet has his age, the side, and "6 weeks, no injury" — three answers you did not have to ask for.

So the call goes further. It is the right knee, front and inside, worse going up stairs and worse after a long drive. No swelling, no locking, no giving way.

He is a taxi driver, ten hours a day, six days a week, and he cannot afford to stop working — he is very clear about that.

And he tells you he came to the desk because he tried to book online twice and gave up both times.
model:
1. Get the desk sheet before you dial. Three of your questions are already answered on it, and reading it first is what turns a repeat interview into a real call.

2. Then ask what the sheet cannot tell you: what makes it worse, and what he does all day. Ten hours in a driving seat is the load and stairs are the symptom.

3. What happens if he stops working. The answer is that he cannot, which is the main constraint on any plan you make. His two failed attempts to book online also tell you something useful — his chart will stay thin unless somebody asks him directly, so do not send him forms.
q5key: Ten hours a day in a driving seat, and worse going up stairs. A good choice shows the driving position or the stair step, so he recognises his own day on the screen.

title: The number is withheld
brief:
New patient. Booked by phone.
Complaint: lower back, "2 weeks, lifted something heavy."
Worse: bending.
The caller withheld their number and gave no other contact detail. Reception has no way to call back.
First appointment tomorrow at 14:00.

q1.prompt: You cannot make the call. What do you do before he arrives tomorrow?
opts: Cancel the appointment until he gives the clinic a contact number.
Ask reception to keep trying, in case the number turns up somewhere.
Write out the questions the call would have asked, and plan the session so the first ten minutes do that job.
Nothing can be done. No number, no call — take the history tomorrow as normal.
q1.why: Some charts can never be improved before the visit, and this is one of them. That is not a reason to shrug — it is a reason to move the call into the start of the session deliberately, on paper, tonight. "Take the history as normal" is what everyone says they will do and it is how the first twenty minutes get eaten by questions in no particular order. Cancelling punishes a man with a two-week lifting injury for a phone setting. Chasing a withheld number gets you nothing and takes reception's time.

reveal:
He arrives on time, and because you decided in advance what the first ten minutes were for, you get everything.

He lifted a sack of cement two weeks ago and felt immediate pain. He is a builder and he has kept working every day since. No leg pain, no numbness, no problem walking.

At worst it is 8 out of 10. He has been taking painkillers bought from a shop, several a day, and does not know what they are.

At the end he explains why the number was withheld: he is between contracts and worried about being chased for money.
model:
1. Plan the call's questions and ask them before you touch him: mechanism, negatives, how bad, what he is taking, what he needs to be able to do.

2. Say out loud at the start what the shape of the session is. A patient who has had no call does not know it begins with talking, and may be expecting hands on his back from the first minute.

3. Accept that you have lost the preparation time and not the information — but only if you decided in advance not to skip it. Shop-bought painkillers several times a day, name unknown, is the piece you would have missed if you had rushed to the plinth.
q5key: The mechanism is lifting a cement sack, and he is still doing it every day. A good choice shows that lift, so he can show you how he is doing it now rather than describe it.

title: His wife booked it
brief:
New patient, 46. Booked by his wife.
Complaint, in her words: "My husband has had back pain for years and will not do anything about it. It is affecting his sleep and his mood. He needs to be seen."
Duration: "years."
Contact number: hers.
First appointment tomorrow at 18:00.

q1.prompt: What do you do before he arrives tomorrow?
opts: Call her back and say that he needs to book his own appointment.
Call, ask to speak to him, and find out whether he actually wants to be there.
Call his wife and take the history from her — she has watched it for years and she booked it.
Plan the session from her description. It is detailed enough to work from.
q1.why: A spouse-booked appointment carries a history in the third person and a motivation nobody has checked. A patient who has been sent behaves completely differently from one who chose to come, and if you do not know which you have, you will build a plan for the wrong man. Her account will be accurate about his mood and silent about his back. Refusing the booking punishes the one person in this who is trying. Expect him to be polite and slightly reluctant on the phone — that is the point of calling.

reveal:
You ask to speak to him and his wife puts him on. He is polite and a little reluctant, and clearly does not think this is necessary.

About eight years, on and off. Worse in the mornings and after long drives — he drives two hours a day. He sleeps badly during the bad weeks, which is what his wife has been watching.

He says he is coming because she arranged it, and that he had assumed years ago that nothing could be done about it.

Then, almost as an afterthought as the call is ending, he mentions that he stopped playing football with his son about a year ago.
model:
1. Get him on the phone, and establish whether he wants to be there. Everything about tomorrow depends on that answer, and his wife cannot give it to you.

2. The ordinary history: how long, what makes it worse, what it does to his sleep. Eight years, worse in the mornings, two hours of driving a day.

3. Ask what he has stopped doing. The line that matters is the one he almost did not say — he stopped playing football with his son. That is his own reason to come back, as opposed to his wife's, and it is the whole difference between one session and a course.
q5key: He has stopped playing football with his son. A good choice shows that, not a spine — putting his own goal on the screen is what makes the session his rather than his wife's.

title: Her mother filled in the form
brief:
New patient, age 14. Booked by her mother, who filled in the form.
Occupation: "a dancer."
Complaint: "Pain in the front of both hips for about 3 months. She says it is fine but I can see her limping after class."
Training: "ballet 5 days a week, plus a competition group on Saturdays."
Goal, in the mother's words: "She has an audition in 8 weeks."
First appointment tomorrow at 17:00.

q1.prompt: What do you do before she arrives tomorrow?
opts: Call and take the history from the mother. She is the one who notices, and the patient is a minor.
Wait until tomorrow and ask them both together in the room.
Call the mother and explain that a 14-year-old training six days a week should reduce her load before she is seen.
Call and speak to the girl herself, with her mother present, and hear her own version.
q1.why: The mother says one thing and the daughter says another — the form itself records the gap, and that gap is the most useful thing on the chart. A young dancer who tells her mother she is "fine" is usually protecting her audition, and she will not correct the record with only her mother speaking. Waiting until the room means the first version you hear is still the mother's, in front of the daughter, which makes it harder for her to disagree. And giving load advice before you have heard from the patient sets the whole thing up as a fight about the audition.

reveal:
You speak to them both, and you make a point of asking the daughter directly.

It is deep in the front of both hips, worse in high kicks and worst after Saturday competition work. And it has been about five months, not three — she corrects her mother on the call.

She has not told her ballet teacher, because she does not want to lose her place in the competition group.

Then the piece her mother did not know: she has been taking painkillers before class, most classes, for several weeks. And she says plainly that she is not missing the audition in eight weeks whatever anyone tells her.
model:
1. Hear the daughter's own version, asked of her directly. Three months becomes five, and that only happened because the question went to the patient.

2. What she has not told anyone, and why. Her teacher does not know, because her place in the competition group depends on it — that is the pressure the whole case sits inside.

3. What she is taking. Painkillers before most classes means she has been training on hips whose warning signals are switched off, and it means your tests tomorrow may look better than the truth. Our form never asks about medication, and her mother could not have told you.
q5key: The pain comes in high kicks and after Saturday competition work. A good choice shows that movement, so she can point to exactly where in the range it hurts.

title: The photographer and the gear
brief:
New patient, 37.
Occupation: "i'm a photographer."
Complaint: right side of the neck and shoulder, "4 months."
Cause, in his words: "carrying gear — my bag is about 12 kg and I have it on one shoulder all day at events."
Worse: end of a shoot day, holding the camera up.
Treated before: "massage every few weeks."
Goal: "get through a wedding season."
First appointment tomorrow at 12:00.

q1.prompt: What do you do before he arrives tomorrow?
opts: He has diagnosed his own mechanism and it is plainly right. Plan manual therapy for a four-month neck.
Call him to confirm the appointment. The chart already has the cause, the side and the aggravating factor.
Call him and find out what a shoot day and the coming season actually demand of him.
He has named the load himself. Tell him on the call to carry the bag on the other shoulder and reduce the weight.
q1.why: It is rare and valuable that a patient names his own loading — only 18 charts in 345 recorded an occupation at all, and this one gives you the weight, the side and the aggravating position. Do not spend that by jumping straight to advice: telling him to swap shoulders before you know what a shoot day is will be politely ignored. Planning manual therapy treats the four months and not the four months ahead. And a confirmation call throws away the one chart where the person has already done half your work.

reveal:
You make the call yourself, and this is what you find out.

Shoot days are ten to twelve hours, three days a week in season. He holds a heavy camera at eye level for long stretches and carries the bag on the right shoulder between every shot.

The massage helps for about two days each time, and he has been going every few weeks for a year.

The last month has been worse. And when you ask, he tells you he has started getting numbness in the right hand at the end of long days — new, in the last few weeks. He mentioned it in passing because he assumed it was normal for the job.

Wedding season runs for the next four months and he cannot turn work down.
model:
1. What a shoot day actually is. Hours, how the camera is held, how the bag is carried, how often. Ten to twelve hours, three days a week, is a very different problem from "carrying gear".

2. What the massage achieves and how long it lasts. Two days of relief, every few weeks, for a year, tells you what has been happening instead of treatment.

3. The screening question our form never asks: any numbness or pins and needles. There is, new, in the right hand at the end of long days. That single answer moves this from a tight neck to a case that needs a neurological screen — and it is the reason the call was worth making.
q5key: He holds a heavy camera at eye level and carries 12 kg on one shoulder all day. A good choice shows one of those two positions, so he recognises his own shoot day.

title: The professional fighter
brief:
New patient, 26.
Occupation: "professional fighter."
Complaint: left knee, "on and off 2 years, bad for 3 weeks."
Worse: kicking, changing direction.
Treated before: "strapping, painkillers, I manage it."
Imaging: "MRI last year, was told it was fine."
Goal: "fight in 5 weeks."
First appointment tomorrow at 08:30.

q1.prompt: What do you do before he arrives tomorrow?
opts: Call him, take the fight as a fixed fact, and find out exactly what "I manage it" means and what his training week does to the knee.
Call him and advise him to withdraw from the fight — five weeks is not enough with a knee like that.
A knee is a knee. Assess it tomorrow as you would any other and let the sport look after itself.
Ask him to send the MRI report before you speak, so you know what you are dealing with.
q1.why: A professional with a date on the calendar will not withdraw because a physiotherapist he has never met suggested it, and leading with that ends the conversation in the first thirty seconds. Take the fight as a fact and work inside it. Treating it as an ordinary knee ignores that his training load is about to double when camp starts. And an MRI from last year that was "fine" tells you about last year — the useful history is what two years of self-management has actually involved, and what has changed in the last three weeks.

reveal:
You make the call yourself, and this is what you find out.

Two years of intermittent pain, but the last three weeks are different. It has swollen twice after sparring, and it caught once when he turned — enough that he had to stop the round.

"I manage it" means strapping it for every single session and taking painkillers before sparring. He has been doing that for most of a year.

He trains twice a day, six days a week. Camp for this fight starts next week and the load goes up from there.

And he has not told his coach how bad it is, because he thinks he would be pulled from the card.
model:
1. What "I manage it" actually involves. Strapping every session and pre-sparring painkillers is a year-long system for hiding a knee, and it is the reason nobody has looked at it.

2. What is different about these three weeks. Swelling twice and catching once are new mechanical events, not a worse ache, and they are the clinical heart of the call.

3. What camp will demand, and who knows. The load rises next week and his coach has no idea. Plan for the fight rather than against it, but say plainly on the call that new swelling and catching need assessing properly before the load goes up.
q5key: It swells after sparring and caught when he turned. A good choice shows the kicking or turning movement, so he can show you the exact moment it happened.

title: The golfer with a date
brief:
New patient, 43.
Occupation: "I am a golfer."
Complaint: left lower back, "6 weeks, came on during a tournament."
Worse: driving the ball, sitting in the car afterwards.
Treated before: "physio at my club, 4 sessions, some improvement."
Imaging: none.
Goal: "a tournament in 3 weeks, and I do not want to lose distance."
First appointment tomorrow at 07:30.

q1.prompt: What do you do before he arrives tomorrow?
opts: Call him and find out exactly what the club physiotherapist did in those four sessions.
Three weeks is plenty. Plan a standard course and confirm the appointment.
Call him and advise skipping the tournament to protect the back.
Call him and get at both halves of that goal line: what the three weeks needs, and what "losing distance" means to him.
q1.why: He has given you a deadline and a fear in the same sentence. The deadline shapes the plan; the fear shapes what he will actually accept and do. A golfer who believes treatment will cost him distance will nod at everything you say and quietly stop doing any of it. The previous treatment is worth asking about, but it is the second question, not the first. A standard course ignores the only date that matters. And advising him to skip the tournament, before he has told you anything, is advice he will not take from a stranger.

reveal:
You make the call yourself, and this is what you find out.

The pain is on the left, at the very end of the swing, and it is worse the day after a round than during it. He plays three rounds a week plus range work and has not reduced anything.

The club physiotherapist's four sessions were massage and heat, which helped for about a day each time.

Then the fear, once you ask about it directly. Two years ago he was told to "swing less hard" by someone treating a different problem. He did it, lost distance, and says it ruined his season. He tells you plainly he would rather play in pain than shorten his swing again.
model:
1. Exactly where in the swing it hurts, and what the day after is like. End of the swing, worse the following day, is a loading pattern rather than an incident.

2. What the previous treatment consisted of and what it achieved. Massage and heat, a day of relief each time, four times — that tells you what tomorrow must not be.

3. What "losing distance" means to him, asked directly. It is not a preference, it is a season he believes he lost. Name it on the call, take it off the table, and be clear that the plan is about how much and how often he loads, not about making him swing softer.
q5key: It hurts at the very end of the swing. A good choice shows that finish position, so he can show you exactly where in it the pain arrives.

title: One joint on the form
brief:
New patient, 41.
Complaint: right wrist, "6 weeks, swollen and stiff in the mornings."
Cause: "I do not know."
Treated before: "no."
Past history: "waiting for hospital tests."
Goal: "get the swelling down."
First appointment tomorrow at 13:00.

q1.prompt: What do you do before she arrives tomorrow?
opts: Call her and ask her to bring whatever the hospital has given her so far.
Call her, find out what the hospital tests are for, and ask whether any other joint is involved.
A swollen, stiff wrist with no cause. Assess and treat it tomorrow as planned.
Call her and postpone the appointment until the hospital results are back.
q1.why: Our form asks about one region, so patients answer about one region — that is the trap in this chart, not the wrist. Swelling with an hour of morning stiffness, in someone already under investigation, is precisely the situation where you must ask whether anything else is affected, and the form will never prompt it. Treating it as a wrist means you never ask. Postponing leaves her with a swollen joint and no contact for weeks. Asking for paperwork is reasonable and gets you a letter, not the two questions that change the appointment.

reveal:
You make the call yourself. The wrist has been swollen for six weeks with about an hour of stiffness every morning before she can use it properly.

Then you ask whether anything else is involved, and the case changes. Both her hands have been stiff in the mornings for months. Her left knee has swollen twice, once badly enough that she could not kneel for a week.

She had not mentioned any of it because she booked about the wrist and thought the rest was separate.

The hospital tests are blood tests for an inflammatory condition, taken last week, with results due in a few days.
model:
1. What the tests are for, and when the results come. Blood tests for an inflammatory condition, due within days, is the frame for everything else.

2. The question our form does not ask: is anything else involved. Two hands and a knee, on top of the wrist, is a completely different appointment from a six-week wrist strain.

3. How long the morning stiffness lasts. Over an hour, in multiple joints, with an active investigation, is a picture that has to be raised with a senior physiotherapist today — so that what you do tomorrow fits alongside the medical work rather than cutting across it.
q5key: She came in thinking she has a wrist problem. A good choice supports explaining why you asked about her other joints — the priority here is the conversation, not the picture.

title: Shoulder, one word
brief:
New patient, 49.
Complaint: left shoulder.
How long: "about 3 weeks."
Cause: "not sure."
Treated before: "went to the hospital."
Goal: "get my arm up again."
First appointment tomorrow at 15:00.

q1.prompt: What do you do before he arrives tomorrow?
opts: Assume it was an X-ray that showed nothing and plan shoulder rehabilitation.
Call him and find out exactly what happened at the hospital, in order.
A three-week shoulder that has already been to hospital. Plan the assessment and confirm the time.
Call him and ask him to bring all his hospital paperwork tomorrow.
q1.why: Patients compress whole medical episodes into three words. "Went to the hospital" can mean a five-minute X-ray or a week of treatment, and until you know which, you do not know what you are treating. Planning the assessment assumes the shoulder is the problem. Asking for paperwork is sensible and still leaves you a day away from the answer — and many patients arrive with nothing. Assuming an X-ray is the most dangerous option on the list, because it is the assumption everybody makes.

reveal:
You call and ask him to take you through it in order: why he went, what they did, what he was given, what happened after.

He went to hospital three weeks ago with a shoulder that was hot and very painful. They gave him three days of antibiotics. He had a fever for three days.

Since the fever settled the pain has changed — it is much less intense, but he cannot lift the arm above shoulder height at all.

He has had no follow-up of any kind. He assumed the hospital had dealt with it and that physiotherapy was simply the next step.
model:
1. What happened at the hospital, in order. Why he went, what they did, what they gave him, what happened next. Nothing else on this call comes close in importance.

2. What has changed since. Less pain but no elevation at all is a change in the picture, not an improvement you can build on.

3. Whether anyone has followed it up. Nobody has. A shoulder treated with antibiotics is a shoulder somebody was worried about, and before any treatment you need to know what for and whether it is resolved — senior physiotherapist and medical review today, which is not the same thing as sending him away.
q5key: He wants his arm to lift again and does not understand what happened to him. A good choice supports the explanation of the next step — the conversation matters more than the picture here.

title: What methods do you use?
brief:
New patient, 39.
Complaint: right hip and groin, "8 months, gradual."
Worse: sitting cross-legged, getting out of the car.
Treated before: "3 physios, 2 chiropractors, an osteopath."
Imaging: "MRI and X-ray, told nothing serious."
Before booking she asked reception a list of questions: what methods we use, whether the physiotherapist has a masters degree, what equipment we have, and whether we do dry needling and shockwave.
First appointment tomorrow at 10:00.

q1.prompt: What do you do before she arrives tomorrow?
opts: Call her and answer her questions properly — methods, qualifications, equipment — since that is what she asked.
She has interviewed the clinic and will be hard work. Keep the call short and factual.
Tell reception to let her know all her questions will be answered at the appointment.
Call her and find out what has actually happened to her across six practitioners and eight months.
q1.why: A patient who checks credentials and equipment before booking has usually been let down repeatedly, and the questionnaire is the symptom rather than the request. Eight months, six practitioners, imaging that showed nothing. Answering the list politely gives her a seventh set of claims to compare and tells her nothing she can use. Writing her off as difficult before you have spoken guarantees it. Deferring everything to the appointment leaves her doing the only thing she knows how to do — comparing techniques on the internet tonight.

reveal:
You make the call yourself, and this is what you find out.

Eight months, deep in the front of the hip and groin, worse sitting cross-legged and getting out of the car. It has not changed at all in that time.

Each of the six gave her a different explanation and a different set of exercises. She has done all of them, properly, and she can list them. Two of the explanations directly contradicted each other.

When you ask what she wants, she says she wants one person to tell her what it is and stay with it. She asked about methods because she genuinely cannot tell the difference between them, and she has run out of ways to choose.
model:
1. What each of the six told her, and what she was given. She is carrying six contradictory explanations and that is the real presenting problem.

2. What has and has not changed in eight months. Nothing has, through six courses of treatment — which is information about the problem, not about her.

3. What she needs from you. The list of questions to reception was never a test of your credentials; it was a person with no remaining way to choose. What she has not had is a clear process: assess her properly, say what you think it is, and agree the next step together.
q5key: She has had six explanations and believes none of them. A good choice is the one clear picture you would use to give her a single explanation she can hold on to.

title: Skip the assessment
brief:
New patient, 25. Ten weeks after knee surgery.
Complaint: "stiff, weak, need to get back to sport."
A note from reception: he asked to skip the assessment and go straight to exercises, saying he has already been assessed twice and does not want to pay to be assessed again.
No operation report. Imaging: "at the hospital."
First appointment tomorrow at 09:30.

q1.prompt: What do you do before he arrives tomorrow?
opts: Call him, find out what the two previous assessments found and what he has been doing since, then explain what you cannot safely do without your own.
Call him and explain that there is no treatment without an assessment. That is how the clinic works.
He has been assessed twice in ten weeks. Respect that and go straight to exercises tomorrow.
Call him and ask him to bring both previous reports and the operation note before you plan anything.
q1.why: His request is not unreasonable on its face — he has paid to be assessed twice already, and being asked a third time feels like being charged for the same thing. But ten weeks after knee surgery, prescribing load without knowing what was repaired or where the knee is now is not something you can safely do. Refusing on policy grounds gives him a rule instead of a reason and he will argue with it. Skipping the assessment gambles with a repair. And asking for paperwork first makes documents the condition of being treated, when the fastest route is simply to ask him what happened.

reveal:
You make the call yourself, and this is what you find out.

The two assessments were both at the hospital, at five weeks and nine weeks. He was told the knee was progressing and handed a sheet each time.

He cannot tell you what was actually repaired. He knows the surgeon's name and nothing else.

He has been doing the exercises from the second sheet. And last week, on his own initiative, he started jogging — since when the knee has been swelling every evening.

He wants to be back playing five-a-side football in a month.
model:
1. What the two assessments actually said, and what he was given. Two sheets and "it is progressing" is not the same as having been assessed for the load he now wants.

2. What he has been doing. He started jogging last week on his own decision and the knee has swelled every evening since. That is the single most useful sentence on this call.

3. What he wants and by when. Five-a-side in a month. Then use his own information to answer his objection: the swelling after new jogging is exactly what twenty minutes of assessment is for, and it is the thing that will otherwise cost him the month.
q5key: He wants to be back playing in a month and does not know what was repaired. A good choice is the picture you would point at to show what the knee is ready for and what comes next.

title: Both sides, and slowly worse
brief:
New patient, 74.
Complaint: "Pins and needles in both hands and both feet. Getting slowly worse."
How long: "years — maybe 10, but worse in the last year."
Worse: "walking any distance."
Treated before: "massage, and a chiropractor a long time ago."
Goal: "walk to the market again."
First appointment tomorrow at 11:30.

q1.prompt: What do you do before he arrives tomorrow?
opts: Book a double session so there is time to assess all four limbs properly.
Refer him straight back to his doctor without calling.
Call him today and screen it carefully: both sides, weakness, unsteadiness, falls, bladder and bowel.
Long-standing pins and needles in an older man. Call to confirm and assess tomorrow as usual.
q1.why: Symptoms on both sides, in arms and legs, progressive over years, with walking distance falling away, is not an ordinary presentation — and it arrived on the chart looking exactly like ordinary numbness in an older patient, which is why it is dangerous. A confirmation call finds nothing. A double session is a decision to find out tomorrow what you could know today. And referring him back without speaking to him leaves a man who has stopped walking to the market with no contact and no plan. This is the case where the call itself changes what happens.

reveal:
You call him today. The pins and needles are constant in both hands and both feet, and they have been getting steadily worse over the last year.

He can manage about five minutes of walking before his legs feel heavy, and it eases when he sits down. It used to be twenty minutes.

Over the last year he has become unsteady, especially in the dark, and he has had two near-falls at home — one on the stairs. He has not told his doctor about the unsteadiness because he assumed it was his age.

No bladder or bowel changes. No problems with his hands beyond the numbness.
model:
1. The screening our form never asks for: both sides, getting worse, any weakness, any unsteadiness, any bladder or bowel change, any falls. Two of those are positive and he has told nobody.

2. The walking distance and what eases it. Five minutes, heavy legs, eased by sitting, down from twenty minutes over a year.

3. Then two things happen today, not tomorrow: escalation to a senior physiotherapist and medical review, and the immediate practical matter of a man at real risk of falling at home. "Normal at my age" is what he has been telling himself for a year.
q5key: He wants to walk to the market and he is frightened of falling. A good choice supports the conversation about why you are asking a doctor to look first — keep it calm and plain.

title: After the head injury
brief:
New patient, 32.
Complaint: right arm and leg, "weak, and numb all the time."
How long: "since the accident 2 years ago."
Past history: "head injury, surgery, 3 weeks in hospital."
Treated before: "rehab at the hospital, stopped a year ago."
Goal: "use my right hand for work again."
First appointment tomorrow at 14:30.

q1.prompt: What do you do before he arrives tomorrow?
opts: Two years on, the picture is settled. Plan a strengthening programme for the right side.
Call him and explain that this needs a neurological specialist rather than our clinic.
Call him and ask him to bring his hospital discharge summary and imaging tomorrow.
Call him and find out what the injury was, what the rehabilitation achieved, and why it stopped.
q1.why: Constant numbness and one-sided weakness after a head injury and surgery is a different case from anything else on this list, and the chart gives you almost none of it. What was damaged, what came back, when it stopped improving, and why the rehabilitation ended are four things you need before you plan a single exercise. Strengthening assumes the problem is strength. Turning him away is both wrong and, after a year of nothing, cruel. Paperwork is useful and secondary — the reason his rehabilitation stopped is not written on any discharge summary.

reveal:
You make the call yourself, and this is what you find out.

The weakness affects his right hand most. He cannot grip small objects, and he cannot hold a pen for more than a minute. The numbness is constant and has not changed for about a year.

The hospital rehabilitation stopped a year ago because his funding ran out, not because he had finished or plateaued. He has done nothing since and he feels he has gone backwards.

He wants to go back to work that needs that hand. And in two years nobody has ever told him whether that is possible — which is, in the end, the actual reason he booked.
model:
1. What the injury and the surgery involved, in his own account. Two years of history that is nowhere on our form.

2. What the rehabilitation achieved, and why it stopped. Funding, not recovery — which means the last year of decline was not inevitable and he does not know that.

3. What he wants, and what he has been told about it. He wants to work with that hand and nobody has answered him. Do not promise recovery and do not close the door: say when you can answer, promise honesty, and name what you would work towards either way.
q5key: His goal is gripping with the right hand for work. A good choice shows a real gripping task from his job, so the session is aimed at that from the first minute.

title: Nothing has ever worked
brief:
New patient, 52. Neck, shoulders and upper back.
She has written at length: a numbered list of everything she has tried over seven years — three physiotherapy courses, acupuncture, dry needling, cupping, two chiropractors, a posture course, an ergonomic chair, injections, three types of pillow — each with a note on why it failed.
The last line: "I have accepted this is just how I am. My husband made me book."
First appointment tomorrow at 16:30.

q1.prompt: What do you do before she arrives tomorrow?
opts: Call her and point out gently that the list shows she never stayed with anything long enough.
Call her, thank her and name one item from the list, then ask what came closest to helping and how long she gave each thing.
Call her and go through the list with her, so she knows you have read every item.
She has tried everything and expects nothing. Keep the plan small and manage her expectations tomorrow.
q1.why: That list is not a treatment history, it is a belief — nothing works and this is permanent — and she has also told you she did not choose to come. Both matter more tomorrow than any of the nine treatments named on it. Reading the list back is what this patient will interrupt, and she will be right to. Managing expectations before you have spoken to her accepts her belief as a diagnosis. And telling her she never stuck with anything, in the first conversation, is true and completely unusable — she will hear that seven years of trying were her own fault.

reveal:
You thank her, name one item from the list so she knows you read it, and ask what came closest to helping.

The answer arrives immediately. A period of swimming, about three years ago, twice a week for four months. It was the only thing that ever made a real difference, and she stopped because the pool closed. She has never put it back.

Then, as you ask how long she gave the others, a pattern appears: two or three weeks each, nine times over.

And she says something that is not on the pages. She is not really in pain all the time. What has happened is that she has stopped expecting anything better.
model:
1. Thank her and name one specific item, then do not recap. With this patient, ten seconds of proof that you read it buys you the whole call.

2. What came closest to helping. In a list of nine failures, the swimming is the most useful sentence in the chart — and it only appears because you asked the question in that direction.

3. How long she gave each thing. Two or three weeks, nine times, is not a woman who never tried; it is a pattern nobody has ever shown her. That, plus one thing that demonstrably worked, is the first reason she has had in seven years to expect something.
q5key: She believes this is permanent and expects nothing. A good choice is whatever helps you show her one thing that can change — the point is to interrupt the belief, not to explain the anatomy.

title: A full history and no pain
brief:
New patient, 47.
Reason for visit: "Full body screening. I have no pain."
She has written three pages anyway: her exercise week in detail, her diet, her sleep hours, a list of every injury since school with dates, her family history of arthritis, two sets of blood results, and a printed summary from a smart watch.
Goal: "I want to know if anything is developing before it becomes a problem."
First appointment tomorrow at 09:00.

q1.prompt: What do you do before she arrives tomorrow?
opts: No pain and no complaint. A short screening session and some general advice will do.
Call her and explain that we treat problems rather than screen people who are well.
Call her, thank her for the pages, and ask the one question they do not answer: what made her book now.
Call her to confirm, then plan a full assessment of every region she has listed.
q1.why: Nobody writes three pages, prints two sets of blood results and attaches watch data because they feel relaxed. There is a specific worry behind this and the chart does not say what it is — the volume of paper is what is hiding it. Assessing every region she listed is a way of spending an hour without ever finding it. A short advice session takes the stated request at face value. And telling her the clinic does not screen well people turns away someone who is, on this evidence, quite frightened.

reveal:
You start to go through her history and she cuts in: "It is all in the document I sent."

So you thank her, name one thing from it, and ask what made her book now rather than last year. That is when it comes out.

Her mother was diagnosed with arthritis at the age she is now, and lost her independence early. She has read that it is hereditary.

And she has noticed that her hands feel stiff for a few minutes each morning. She has been watching them for months, every morning, and she has told nobody — not her husband, not her doctor. That is why she booked, and it is the one thing that is not in the three pages.
model:
1. Thank her and name something specific from the pages, then stop reading them back. This patient will interrupt you, and the interruption is the warning.

2. What made her book now. Not the diet, not the watch data — a family history and months of quiet watching.

3. What she has actually noticed herself. A few minutes of morning stiffness in her hands, unreported to anyone. She asked for a screening because "I am frightened of getting my mother's arthritis" is very hard to say to a stranger. Once she has said it, tomorrow has an obvious job — and a general screening hour would have missed it entirely.
q5key: She is comparing herself to her mother and watching her own hands every morning. A good choice is the simple picture you would use to explain what her morning stiffness means and what she can influence.
